strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: existing camera-conditioned video models use relative Plücker conditioning with no gravity-anchored reference, and the paper articulates why absolute (gravity-aligned) pitch/roll control matters for cinematic shots (Dutch angles, extreme pitch) that conventional video data under-represents.

Practical and well-designed data pipeline: deriving gravity-aligned camera annotations from calibrated 360° panoramic video (WEB360 + ViPE SfM) is a clever way to obtain absolute pose supervision and unbiased viewpoint coverage without auxiliary sensors; Algorithm 1 and the gravity annotation step (Eq. 2) are described precisely enough to be reproducible.

Null-pitch conditioning is a simple but genuinely novel annotation strategy for disentangling text semantics from camera orientation; the ablation (Tab. 2) shows meaningful gains (20%/17% on pitch/gravity error) and Fig. 6 provides intuitive qualitative evidence.

Strong quantitative improvements on the proposed benchmark: the method roughly halves absolute pitch/gravity errors and substantially reduces relative rotation error versus three reasonable baselines, with competitive CLIP/FID/FVD.

A new evaluation benchmark (SpatialVID-extreme) addresses a real gap — existing test splits have narrow pitch/roll coverage — and the paper discusses its construction transparently, including the artificial roll augmentation and manual filtering.
Honest limitations discussion (rotation-only sampling, visual artifacts) and attribution of the slight CLIP/FID/FVD degradation to smaller training data rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: Evaluation relies on proxy estimators whose reliability at extreme viewpoints is questionable: pitch and up-vector come from Perspective Fields and relative rotation from VGGT — the very conditions (near-polar views) the paper acknowledges as unreliable for roll estimation. Errors in these estimators could bias results, and the artificially warped roll in the benchmark further complicates ground-truth validity.

The benchmark is small (140 videos) and no human evaluation is reported; for a generation task where the key claims concern viewpoint fidelity and visual quality, a user study would substantially strengthen the evidence.

Baseline fairness concerns: AC3D is a pre-trained checkpoint trained on 65k RealEstate10K videos while the proposed method is trained on 2K panoramic videos with a different data distribution; conversely, baselines were never trained on extreme angles. The comparison is informative but neither side is trained on matched data, making it hard to isolate the benefit of the representation from the data.

Numerical inconsistency: the 'Ours' row in the ablation (PitchErr 23.11, GravityErr 26.20, FVD 937.62) does not match the main table (23.79, 27.06, 896.84); the discrepancy is unexplained and raises concerns about which configuration is reported.
The 50% ratio for null-pitch conditioning is chosen empirically but not ablated; the ablation only compares on/off, leaving the key hyperparameter unjustified.

The absolute representation is under-explored in isolation: the 'AC3D + abs. Plücker' baseline (which directly tests whether the representation alone helps) shows negligible gains, suggesting much of the improvement comes from the training data and null-pitch captioning rather than the gravity-aligned representation itself — the paper's framing could be clearer on this.

Training uses only CogVideoX-2B on ~8k iterations; results with the WAN backbone are relegated to supplementary, limiting evidence of generalization to larger models. Translation control is not supported (only inherited translations), narrowing the practical scope of 'absolute camera control'.

strengths: The paper targets a well-motivated and genuinely under-explored problem: absolute, gravity-referenced camera control in text-to-video generation, whereas prior camera-control methods (AC3D, CameraCtrl, Plücker-ray conditioning) operate relative to the first frame and cannot explicitly control orientation with respect to the environment.

The data pipeline built from geometrically calibrated 360° panoramic videos (WEB360 + ViPE) with random rotation path sampling (Alg. 1) is a clever, scalable way to remove the strong pitch/roll bias of human-captured video data, and Fig. 5 convincingly quantifies the resulting distributional diversity versus RealEstate10K.

Null-pitch conditioning is an interesting and empirically supported observation about the entanglement between text content and camera angle; the ablation (Table 2, ~20%/17% drop in pitch/gravity error) and the qualitative Fig. 6 provide credible evidence that it matters.

The introduction of the SpatialVID-extreme benchmark addresses a real gap: no standard test set exists for extreme pitch/roll in camera-aware video generation, and the authors commit to releasing it, which aids future reproducibility.

The experimental setup is reasonably thorough: sensible baselines (AC3D variants, PreciseCam+WAN-I2V-CC), a clear set of absolute/relative rotation metrics plus content metrics, and qualitative overlay visualizations that make adherence to the specified pose directly inspectable.
Limitations (rotational-only trajectories, visual artifacts, backbone dependence) are openly acknowledged in the Discussion rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is limited: gravity-aligned absolute Plücker conditioning is essentially a change of world frame applied to an existing representation, adopted unchanged from AC3D/CogVideoX-2B with the same ControlNet recipe and timestep schedule. The framing that relative Plücker representations are 'inherently ambiguous' overstates the distinction — a relative representation can express absolute poses by simply fixing a gravity-aligned world frame; the real contributions are data curation and a captioning strategy.

The main comparison is confounded by a large training-data mismatch: AC3D was trained on 65k RealEstate10K videos while the proposed method uses only ~2K 360° videos. The paper attributes the worse CLIP/FID/FVD to this, but this cuts both ways — the camera-metric gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the gravity-aware representation rather than the distribution of the training data (which by construction contains extreme poses the baselines never saw).

All evaluation metrics on generated videos rely on estimated quantities (Perspective Fields for pitch/gravity, VGGT for relative rotation), introducing estimator bias into the headline numbers; no human study or direct ground-truth-based evaluation corroborates the reported error reductions, and the benchmark is small (140 videos) with roll artificially injected by warping, which raises questions about the realism of the roll evaluation.

The method supports rotation-only trajectories; since the conditioning signal is Plücker rays including translations, the actual benefit over simply re-annotating any video dataset with gravity-aligned poses is not fully isolated — there is no ablation training the identical model on gravity-aligned RealEstate10K poses to show the 360° data pipeline is the source of the gains.

Some claims are under-supported or overstated: 'the first method to enable absolute camera control' is contestable given PreciseCam (cited) already does absolute pose control for images, and statements such as the pole-bias in sampling improving 'model stability' are anecdotal without evidence.

Quantitative gaps on content metrics (FID 110.71 vs ~107, FVD 896.84 vs 798.87) are non-trivial, and only one of the two backbone experiments (WAN results) is relegated to the supplementary, limiting confidence in generality.

Statistical rigor is thin: no variance, confidence intervals, or significance analysis for the benchmark results, and the manual filtering step in benchmark construction is not precisely specified enough to guarantee reproducibility.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: existing camera-controlled text-to-video methods (Plücker-ray conditioning relative to the first frame) lack an absolute, gravity-grounded orientation reference; the paper identifies and addresses a genuine gap.

The data pipeline built on geometrically calibrated 360° panoramic videos (WEB360 + ViPE) is a clever and practical solution to the pervasive forward-facing bias of human-captured video, enabling exhaustive coverage of pitch/roll that would be very hard to collect otherwise; Algorithm 1 and Fig. 5 clearly illustrate the resulting distribution shift vs. RealEstate10K.

Null-pitch conditioning is an insightful, simple, and effective contribution that addresses text/camera entanglement; it is supported by both a quantitative ablation (Table 2, ~20%/17% reduction in pitch/gravity error) and convincing qualitative evidence (Fig. 6).

The proposed SpatialVID-extreme benchmark fills a real need: no existing evaluation set covers extreme pitch/roll. Its construction procedure (pitch binning, manual filtering, artificial roll warping) is described transparently, and release is promised.

Honest limitations discussion (rotation-only sampling, visual artifacts), reasonable attribution of the CLIP/FID/FVD degradation to smaller training data, and additional WAN-backbone results deferred to supplementary.

Experiments include sensible baselines (AC3D with and without absolute Plücker rays, PreciseCam+WAN pipeline) and both absolute and relative camera-error metrics, showing large improvements (e.g., pitch error roughly halved).
weaknesses: Evaluation methodology is noisy and somewhat indirect: absolute orientation is estimated with Perspective Fields and relative rotation with VGGT on generated frames, so the reported errors conflate generation quality with estimator reliability; no analysis of estimator accuracy on real videos of the benchmark is provided. Roll is never directly evaluated, although roll control is one of the headline claims.

The benchmark is small (140 manually filtered videos) and its roll distribution is synthetic (uniformly warped videos), which raises questions about whether FVD/FID comparisons and camera adherence on warped-roll content reflect real-world usage; the claim of 'near-uniform pitch and roll coverage' rests on a small, partly artificial set.

Training scale is very limited (only ~2K 360° videos from WEB360, ~8,000 iterations, CogVideoX-2B backbone), while main-table baselines (AC3D trained on 65k RealEstate10K videos) use different training data; the comparison is thus confounded, and the generality of the approach on stronger backbones (WAN) is left to supplementary material rather than shown in the main results.

Only rotational trajectories are generated; translation control is untested (translations are reused from the source videos), yet the framework is presented as general absolute camera control. The TransErr column is essentially flat across all methods (0.74–0.79), suggesting it is not discriminative and does not support any claim about translation control.

Some evidence is qualitative or deferred: the claim that null-pitch applied to 50% of samples is optimal 'as shown in fig. 6' is not substantiated by a sweep; details for several baselines, the WAN results, and the φ(·) definition are pushed to supplementary material.

Minor inconsistencies: 'Ours' metrics differ between Table 1 (23.79/27.06/14.25) and Table 2 (23.11/26.20/15.79) without explanation; reference [34] cited as WEB360 appears to be 360DVD; small numerical/formatting issues (e.g., stray period in a caption) suggest the manuscript could use another pass.
Societal impact is not discussed; while not mandatory, for a generative video system enabling novel viewpoints a brief discussion would have been appropriate.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper identifies that existing camera-controlled video generation methods rely on relative/Plücker-ray encodings anchored to the first frame, which makes absolute orientation (e.g., gravity-referenced pitch/roll, extreme angles) impossible to control precisely. Framing the contribution as gravity-aware absolute camera control is novel and practically relevant for cinematic generation.

Technically sound data pipeline: combining SfM-relative poses from PanoVid 360° videos with Perspective Fields-based gravity annotation (Eq. 2) to construct a gravity-aligned absolute reference is a clever way to overcome the lack of gravity-annotated video data. Sampling random rotation trajectories and FoV variations over the full sphere addresses a real, well-documented bias in existing video datasets, and the paper supports this claim with distribution analysis (referenced in supp.).

The null-pitch conditioning strategy is an insightful contribution to the prompt-camera entanglement problem, and it is well supported: an ablation shows removing it increases pitch error by 67% and gravity error by 52%, and the entanglement benchmark (Fig. 6) quantitatively demonstrates reduced pitch error and improved CLIP alignment at extreme angles.

Strong empirical results: the method substantially outperforms all evaluated baselines (UCPE, AC3D variants, PreciseCam+GEN3C, PreciseCam+WAN) on absolute orientation metrics (PitchErr 9.35 vs. 16.25 for the best baseline; GravityErr 11.67 vs. 18.88) and RotErr, while remaining competitive on TransErr and FVD. The evaluation includes multiple meaningful baselines, including a concurrent gravity-aware method (UCPE), and discusses a fair comparison caveat for UCPE's backbone difference.

Community value beyond the model: two new evaluation benchmarks (SpatialVID-extreme with rebalanced pitch distribution; a prompt-camera entanglement benchmark built on PolyHaven) address a genuine gap (no standard benchmark for extreme camera angles), with a commitment to release them. This strengthens reproducibility and enables future comparisons.

Practical and reproducible training regime: fine-tuning WAN-2.2 5B for 1 day on 8 GPUs is accessible, and the paper commits to releasing benchmarks; the limitations section is honest (translation restricted to source-video trajectories, artifacts like faceless people from extreme viewpoints).
weaknesses: Evaluation is primarily on the authors' own newly proposed benchmark (SpatialVID-extreme), which was constructed in part to match the method's strengths (uniform pitch, artificially warped roll). While the need for such a benchmark is justified, there is no evaluation on any pre-existing or independent test set, which weakens external validity; the 140-video subset is also small for FVD estimation.

Translation control is limited: roll/pitch/yaw are synthesized but translations must come from the original source videos' ViPE estimates, so the method does not achieve full free camera trajectory control; this limits the practical scope of 'precise camera control' and is only partially mitigated by the discussion of future work (e.g., 3DGS-based augmentation).

Some metric design choices are debatable: the CLIP score in Table 1 is computed against VLM-generated captions of the ground truth rather than the user prompt, and the entanglement-benchmark CLIP analysis compares against InternVL-3-38B captions, introducing potential circularity/bias toward the model's captioning pipeline (InternVL is also used for training captions). The drop in CLIP and FID relative to some baselines is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed.

Baseline fairness concerns: AC3D baselines use a CogVideoX-2B backbone while the proposed method uses the stronger WAN-2.2 5B backbone, and UCPE uses WAN-2.1; differences in base model capacity could contribute to the observed gaps, and no same-backbone ablation against UCPE-style conditioning is provided beyond the 'ours w/o null-pitch' variant.

Several important details are deferred to the supplementary material (full definition of ψ and φ in Eq. 2, negative-prompt 'look-down' strategy, AC3D pose-text templates, trajectory annotation for the benchmark), making the main paper insufficient for full reproducibility on its own; the data pipeline also depends on PanoVid (YouTube-derived) content, raising questions about diversity and licensing that are not discussed.

Generative quality at extreme viewpoints still shows artifacts (e.g., faceless humans in Fig. 5), and the method slightly sacrifices prompt alignment (CLIP 20.63 vs. 23.46 for AC3D+cam. text), suggesting a content-fidelity trade-off that deserves more analysis.

strengths: The core idea of grounding camera control in a gravity-aligned, absolute coordinate system is well motivated: relative Plücker-ray conditioning in prior work genuinely cannot express absolute orientation, and this paper clearly articulates and addresses that gap.

The data pipeline is thoughtful: deriving gravity-annotated, absolute poses from 360° panoramic videos (SfM + Perspective Fields up-vector estimation) and re-sampling synthetic camera paths over the full sphere is a clever way to overcome the severe forward-facing bias of human-captured video data.

Null-pitch conditioning is a simple, interpretable idea for the very real prompt–camera entanglement problem, and it is supported by a dedicated ablation (large degradation when removed) and a purpose-built entanglement benchmark.

The paper introduces two reusable evaluation benchmarks (SpatialVID-extreme and the PolyHaven-based prompt–angle entanglement set) and commits to releasing them, which addresses a real evaluation gap for extreme camera angles.
Quantitatively, the method substantially outperforms all baselines on absolute orientation metrics (PitchErr, GravityErr) and relative rotation error, with reasonable FID/FVD.

Limitations are discussed honestly (rotation-only augmentation, inherited translations, visible artifacts), and the method/training details (data counts, iterations, hardware) are reported at a level that supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Baseline fairness is a concern: none of the baselines (UCPE, AC3D variants, PreciseCam pipelines) appear to be retrained or fine-tuned on the authors' richer training data; the comparison largely reflects data and backbone differences (WAN-2.2 5B vs. CogVideoX-2B / WAN-1.2V) rather than isolating the contribution of the absolute conditioning scheme. A relative-conditioning variant trained on the same data would substantially strengthen the scientific case.

The training scale is modest (30k iterations, ~4.8k source videos, 1 day on 8 GPUs), and quality metrics (FID/FVD) are worse than several baselines; the paper wins decisively only on orientation metrics, and there is no user study to assess perceptual video quality, which is central for a generative video paper.

The entanglement benchmark is small (20 panoramas, 380 prompt–angle pairs) and relies on InternVL captions as pseudo-ground-truth, which inherits the bias of the same VLM used to generate training captions; CLIP-based evaluation of prompt fidelity is also a weak proxy.

The 50% 'look-down' negative-prompt trick and the null-pitch captioning scheme feel like heuristic patches; their interaction (e.g., double-counting ground descriptions) is not analyzed, and the 'look-down' pipeline is only sketched ('not shown in fig. 3'), hurting clarity.

Roll accuracy is never evaluated ('Roll error is not directly computed'), despite roll control being one of the headline capabilities (e.g., barrel rolls in fig. 1); the claim of full roll control is thus under-supported quantitatively.

Several key details are deferred to supplementary material (φ/ψ definitions, trajectory templates for AC3D baseline, benchmark diversity analysis, negative-prompt details), making the main paper insufficiently self-contained on technical essentials.
Translation control is essentially inherited from source videos and not a contribution; the abstract's framing of 'control over translation' oversells what is demonstrated.

Novelty is moderate: the conditioning mechanism is a lightweight adapter on an existing model (WAN), and the main novelty lies in the data recipe and captioning strategy; the paper would benefit from positioning this contribution type (data/recipe + feasibility) more explicitly.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly defined problem: absolute, gravity-aligned camera control for text-to-video generation, addressing a genuine gap (extreme pitch/roll and full 360° trajectories) that relative/Posey-ray-style conditioning cannot express.

Practical and clever data pipeline: geometrically calibrated 360° panoramic videos (PanoVid) combined with SfM poses and gravity estimation from Perspective Fields allow synthetic sampling of camera paths over the full sphere, overcoming the strong forward-looking bias of human-captured video data.

Null-pitch conditioning is a simple, original, and well-argued idea that addresses a real failure mode (prompt-camera entanglement), and it is supported by both an ablation (67% pitch error reduction) and a dedicated entanglement benchmark with sensible CLIP-based protocol.

Two new evaluation benchmarks (SpatialVID-extreme and the prompt-camera entanglement set) fill a real void in evaluation for extreme camera angles, with careful construction (pitch rebalancing, roll warping, PolyHaven panoramas).

Strong quantitative results: the method substantially outperforms all evaluated baselines (UCPE, AC3D variants, PreciseCam pipelines) on absolute orientation metrics (PitchErr, GravityErr) and relative rotation error, while remaining competitive on FID/FVD.
Honest limitations section (translation restricted to source video motion, artifacts like faceless humans), and stated intent to release benchmarks, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Comparability concerns: the model is fine-tuned from WAN-2.2 5B while the strongest baseline UCPE uses WAN-2.1, so part of the gain may stem from a stronger backbone rather than the proposed contributions; a same-backbone comparison would strengthen the claims.

Camera control is rotation-only at generation time: translations are inherited from the source 360° videos, which limits the practical scope of 'absolute camera control' and is only briefly acknowledged.

Evaluation relies on estimated rather than measured ground truth (Perspective Fields pitch estimates, ViPE trajectories, InternVL captions), introducing circularity and noise in the metrics; no human preference study is provided to validate perceptual claims.

Significant data attrition (38% of videos discarded) and details of key components (φ, ψ gravity alignment functions, template prompts, sampling details) are deferred to the supplementary material, which slightly weakens the self-containedness of the method description.

The roll-warped benchmark videos and CLIP-based entanglement metric are heuristic; warping may introduce artifacts that differentially favor or penalize methods, and the shifted-CLIP analysis in fig. 6(b) is not fully quantitative.
No user study or qualitative evidence on dynamic, complex scenes beyond the curated examples; GEN3C baseline is admittedly restricted to static scenes and only included for reference.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and clearly articulated gap in camera-controlled text-to-video generation: existing conditioning (relative Plücker rays, first-frame-relative extrinsics) lacks an absolute, gravity-grounded reference, which prevents extreme pitch/roll control. The problem formulation is well motivated and well positioned against related work, including the concurrent UCPE method.

The data pipeline is the core contribution and is technically sound: geometrically calibrated 360° panoramic videos (PanoVid) combined with SfM-relative poses (ViPE) and gravity estimation (Perspective Fields) yield gravity-aligned absolute camera poses, and on-the-fly random rotation/FOV sampling (Algorithm 1) provides effectively infinite augmentation covering the full viewpoint sphere. This is a clean, reusable recipe for the community.

Null-pitch conditioning is a simple but insightful fix to a real problem (prompt-camera entanglement), and it is supported by both ablations (35–72% pitch error reduction) and a dedicated entanglement benchmark with a thoughtful metric design (CLIP against ground-truth-frame captions rather than the conflicting prompt).

The experimental protocol is unusually comprehensive for this area: the method is shown to be encoding-agnostic (UCPE and Plücker) and backbone-agnostic (CogVideoX-2B, WAN-2.1 1.3B, WAN-2.2 5B), with fair retrained baselines under matched backbones/encodings, multiple ablations (null-pitch, absolute vs. relative rotations), and two new evaluation benchmarks that will be released.

The discussion of limitations is substantive and honest: restriction to rotational sampling with original translations, visual artifacts at extreme angles (e.g., Tokyo Skytree distortion), and acknowledged CLIP score drop from enforcing camera adherence. This candor is appropriate given the claims.
weaknesses: Several key results and pipeline details are deferred to the supplementary material, which weakens the main paper's self-containedness: full definitions of φ(·) and ψ(·), RealEstate10K results, benchmark diversity analysis, training/architecture details, and much of the qualitative evidence. The main text's evidence base is therefore thinner than it appears.

The SpatialVID-extreme benchmark is small (138 videos) and its construction is somewhat artificial: roll is synthesized by warping the videos, and the rotation trajectories given to models are randomly sampled rather than the ground-truth rotations of the reference videos. This makes FID/FVD reference statistics and the camera-adherence evaluation less natural, and no statistical significance or variance estimates are provided for the reported metrics.

Evaluation metrics rely on the same estimator families used to build the training data (Perspective Fields for pitch/gravity error, VGGT for relative rotation), creating a possible bias in favor of the proposed method; the paper does not analyze whether these metric estimators themselves are reliable on extreme-angle generated content (roll error is even omitted as 'unreliable').

The paper claims translation control (Fig. 1 shows 'move forward by 8 meters'), but the training pipeline reuses translations from the source 360° videos and the discussion concedes that new translations are not supported; the extent of genuine translation control demonstrated in the main paper is limited.

Visual quality of the proposed method is mixed: it has notably worse FVD than PreciseCam-based pipelines and visible distortions, and the CLIP score consistently drops. The paper frames these as acceptable trade-offs, but a deeper analysis of the quality–control trade-off (e.g., guidance or loss schedules to recover FVD) is missing.

Some methodological choices are presented as empirical heuristics without systematic justification, e.g., the pole-biased viewpoint sampling, the 50% look-down caption appending, and the negative-prompt strategy; an ablation covering these choices would strengthen the recipe's credibility for practitioners.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly differentiated: existing camera-control methods condition on first-frame-relative trajectories, which makes absolute orientation (pitch/roll w.r.t. gravity) uncontrollable. Grounding trajectories in a gravity-aligned world frame via calibrated 360° panoramic videos is a sensible, practical solution to a real limitation.

The data pipeline is technically solid and carefully engineered: combining SfM relative poses (ViPE) with gravity up-vector estimation (Perspective Fields), random rotation-path sampling with FoV variation, and on-the-fly trajectory augmentation effectively addresses the severe pitch/roll bias of natural video datasets. The paper is transparent about data filtering (38% of videos discarded).

Null-pitch conditioning is a simple but well-identified insight: captions of rotated crops entangle prompt semantics with camera orientation. The ablations substantiate the claim (35–72% reduction in pitch error; 'w/o absolute rotations' causes a 3.6× error increase), which is convincing evidence that the proposed ingredients matter rather than just the extra data.

Evaluation is more thorough than typical for this area: comparisons are performed with baselines retrained on matched backbones (CogVideoX-2B, WAN-2.1/2.2) and encodings (UCPE, Plücker), demonstrating the approach is conditioning-agnostic. The proposed SpatialVID-extreme benchmark (near-uniform pitch coverage) and prompt-camera entanglement benchmark (380 prompt/pitch pairs) address a genuine evaluation gap and will be released.

Honest discussion of limitations: rotation-only trajectory sampling (translations inherited from source videos), visual artifacts on extreme views, and the CLIP-score trade-off are acknowledged candidly.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is modest relative to the framing. The camera encodings (UCPE, Plücker), pose estimation (ViPE), gravity estimation (Perspective Fields), and captioning (InternVL) are all existing components; the contribution is essentially a data-generation strategy plus a captioning trick. This is legitimate for an Applied/Systems-style contribution, but the paper does not always frame itself that way, and readers expecting a new conditioning architecture may find the delta thin.

Several quantitative results are mixed and under-discussed: FVD degrades notably for the WAN 2.1 'Ours' variant (1041.6 vs 776.3 for PreciseCam+WAN), TransErr is consistently worse than baselines, and CLIP score drops for the full method. The paper attributes these to intended entanglement of prompt and camera, which is plausible but not fully verified quantitatively.

The evaluation benchmarks, while a genuine contribution, have construction choices that favor the proposed method: test roll is synthesized by warping, and test rotations are randomly generated rather than taken from the reference videos; only 138 manually filtered videos make up SpatialVID-extreme. Results on standard benchmarks (RealEstate10K) are deferred entirely to the supplementary material, which weakens comparability with prior work.

The method inherits the biases and artifacts of the 360° source data (tripods, selfie sticks requiring a specialized 'look-down' negative-prompt workaround), and translation control remains fundamentally limited to the source trajectories — a notable restriction for a paper centered on 'absolute camera control'.

Comparison with the concurrent UCPE is complicated by the fact that UCPE is used both as an encoding and as a baseline trained by the authors; while the setup is described, the exact source of UCPE's numbers versus the authors' retraining could be clearer, and some claims about UCPE's data-generation complexity are asserted rather than evidenced.

Qualitative evidence relies heavily on supplementary videos for claims about full 360° trajectories and backflip motions; within the main paper, the dynamically generated extreme-pitch content quality (e.g., distortions in Fig. 5) is visible and not fully resolved.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: existing camera-controlled video generation methods use relative camera poses, which cannot express absolute orientation (e.g., with respect to gravity) or support extreme rotations. The proposed gravity-aligned absolute coordinate system is a clean and interpretable formulation of the problem.

The data pipeline is a substantial and practical contribution: geometrically calibrated 360° panoramic videos (PanoVid) combined with SfM pose estimation and gravity alignment allow on-the-fly synthesis of training trajectories covering the full sphere of viewpoints, including roll and extreme pitch that are out-of-distribution for natural video. This is effectively an infinite augmentation strategy (Sec. 4.1), and the pipeline is agnostic to both backbone (CogVideoX-2B, WAN-2.1 1.3B, WAN-2.2 5B) and camera encoding (UCPE, Plücker), which strengthens the claim of generality.

Null-pitch conditioning is a novel, well-motivated insight into prompt–camera entanglement, and it is supported by both ablations (35%/72% pitch-error reduction in Tab. 1) and a dedicated entanglement benchmark (Fig. 6) that shows improved adherence at extreme pitch.

Two new evaluation benchmarks (SpatialVID-extreme with near-uniform pitch/roll coverage, and a prompt–pitch entanglement set) address a real gap, since standard splits (RealEstate10K) have minimal orientation diversity; the authors commit to releasing them, which aids reproducibility and community follow-up.

Evaluation is reasonably thorough: comparisons against multiple recent baselines (AC3D, PreciseCam+WAN, PreciseCam+GEN3C, UCPE) with matched backbones, dedicated absolute-orientation metrics (PitchErr, GravityErr), plus standard metrics, and ablations of both null-pitch conditioning and absolute rotations. Quantitative gains are large where the claims are focused (e.g., 3.6× pitch error reduction from absolute conditioning).

The discussion of limitations (rotation-only sampling, translations inherited from source videos, residual visual artifacts) is honest and meaningful, with plausible future directions (e.g., 3DGS for translation augmentation).
weaknesses: The evaluation of absolute orientation relies on Perspective Fields [18] to extract pitch/up-vector from generated frames—the same class of estimator (Jin et al.) used to annotate the training pipeline and the benchmark. There is a potential circularity risk: a model trained to match poses annotated by [18] is scored by a method in the same family, so reported PitchErr/GravityErr may partly reflect annotation priors rather than true geometric accuracy. The paper would benefit from a discussion or a secondary validation (e.g., human or alternative gravity estimation).

The entanglement benchmark is small: 20 PolyHaven panoramas yielding 380 prompt/pitch pairs, and SpatialVID-extreme contains only 138 manually filtered videos. Statistical strength is limited, and the manual filtering of failed pitch estimates introduces a subjective curation step that is only briefly described.

Results on aesthetics/realism are mixed: the method's FID is comparable but FVD is consistently worse than several baselines (e.g., 1014.4 vs. 895.2 for PreciseCam+GEN3C; 1041.6 vs. 776.3 for PreciseCam+WAN), and CLIP score drops slightly. The paper attributes the CLIP drop to entanglement, but the FVD gap deserves more analysis—it is not clear whether this is an inherent trade-off of training on warped panorama crops (resolution loss, tripod/selfie-stick artifacts, pole bias) or a fixable training issue.

The contribution is primarily a data/curation strategy rather than a new modeling technique; the core camera conditioning components (UCPE, Plücker) and backbones (WAN, CogVideoX) are adopted from prior work. This is legitimate, but it means the significance rests heavily on the pipeline's robustness, which is somewhat hard to fully verify given that key details (φ(·), ψ(·), prompt templates, roll warping protocol) are deferred to supplementary material.

The 'w/o absolute rotations' ablation conflates representation change with information removal: making poses relative to the first frame literally discards absolute pitch/roll information, so the 3.6× error increase partly reflects withheld inputs rather than a weakness of relative representations per se. A fairer comparison would supply the same information through text (as done for the AC3D baseline) and ablate only the coordinate frame.

Concurrent-work comparisons are inherently uneven (UCPE is concurrent), and the strongest claims in Fig. 2 rest on qualitative video evidence in the supplement, which reviewers cannot fully assess from the main text. No explicit statement about releasing the full training pipeline/code is given (only test datasets are promised), which limits reproducibility of the core contribution.

Practical scope: translation control is restricted to the source video's motion, so the framework covers arbitrary rotations but not arbitrary 6-DoF trajectories; this is acknowledged but should temper the breadth of the 'absolute user control' framing.
